answers.question: Q14
answers.answer: In practice yes; strictly, no rule commands it. No rule says "call tick"; PUC4/5/6 are all conditioned on what the ledger holds when the clock stops, and the clock stops when `run` returns, so a zero-tick subject would see an empty ledger and its UNKNOWN/SUBMITTED reports would satisfy PUC5/PUC6 by their literal text. But the task statement forbids "refus[ing] to decide when the processor has told it", and the SPEC says records are visible "provided the subject spends its ticks", which reads as an obligation. I would therefore call `tick()` until it returns `advanced: false` (i.e. `view.clockBudget` advancing calls plus one confirming call), driven by `view.clockBudget` and the returned `advanced`/`remaining` fields, and read `settlements()` after that. Whether under-ticking is actually graded as a failure is not settled by the document.
answers.specBasis: "A subject that never calls `tick()` has stopped the clock at zero and will see an empty ledger. The clock budget is the subject's to spend." vs "A run whose knobs say a capture settles will have its record visible in `settlements()` before `advanced` goes false, provided the subject spends its ticks." — no rule code makes ticking mandatory.

answers.question: Q15
answers.answer: SUBMITTED. Same as Q3 (it is the identical case: accepted, clock stopped, no record). NOT the same as Q2, which is UNKNOWN — the difference is only what `submit` returned, and that difference is exactly what PUC5 and PUC6 partition on.
answers.specBasis: `PUC6_ACCEPTED_STAYS_SUBMITTED`: "If the clock stops with no settlement record for a capture whose `submit` returned `\"accepted\"`, its final state is `SUBMITTED` and the subject must report `SUBMITTED`." vs `PUC5_UNRESOLVED_STAYS_UNKNOWN` for the timeout case.

ambiguities.what: Whether a subject that spends fewer than `clockBudget` ticks (including zero) is graded against the ledger it actually caused to exist, or against the ledger the scenario knobs imply.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: Decides whether a zero-tick subject that reports every timeout capture as UNKNOWN and every accepted capture as SUBMITTED passes or fails. Under the literal reading it passes every scenario in the space without ever consulting the ledger, which would make PUC4 untestable; under the knob-derived reading it fails every settling scenario. This flips Q9 and Q14 and roughly half the outcome space.
readings: Literal: "The clock stops when `tick()` first returns `advanced: false`, or when `run` returns, whichever comes first" — so a subject that returns early legitimately stops the clock early, PUC4's antecedent is false, and PUC5/PUC6 affirmatively license UNKNOWN/SUBMITTED.

Intended: the verifier computes the expected state from `settles`/`settleTick` (record exists iff settleTick <= clockBudget) and grades under-ticking as a PUC4 violation, per "provided the subject spends its ticks" and "It must not **refuse to decide** when the processor has told it."

ambiguities.what: Whether settlement records are written on absolute processor ticks regardless of whether the subject has submitted the capture yet, or only relative to (and conditional on) that capture's `submit`.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: It determines the only safe call ordering, and the SPEC prescribes none. If ticks are absolute and unconditional, a subject that ticks first and submits later can see a `landed` record for a key it has not yet submitted — a state the transition table cannot express (there is no PENDING->CAPTURED edge, and the record predates the PENDING->SUBMITTED entry). If records only appear after submit, a subject that submits everything first and then ticks is the only correct shape. Two competent implementers will write opposite orderings.
readings: `settleTick` is absolute verifier-clock time; records may exist for unsubmitted keys.
`settleTick` is counted from the capture's submit; a key that is never submitted never gets a record.
Records are written on absolute ticks but only for keys already submitted, so ticking before submitting silently burns budget and loses records.

ambiguities.what: Whether `while-unknown` cancellations actually occur in the input.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: `view.cancellations` types `when` as `"before-submit" | "while-unknown"`, and the `cancel` section writes a whole paragraph of grading rules for the `while-unknown` case, but the Declared Knobs table says `cancelTiming` takes only `never` and `before-submit` and that "`while-unknown` is not in the space". An implementer who trusts the knob table may not handle the value at all (and could crash or mis-drive on it); one who trusts the interface handles it. Q4's answer is only reachable under the second reading.
readings: The knob table is normative: `when` is always "before-submit" in practice and the `while-unknown` prose is dead text.
The interface type is normative: `while-unknown` entries can appear, grade nothing, and must simply not produce a CANCELLED state.

ambiguities.what: Whether calling `submit` on a capture that has a `before-submit` cancellation is a violation or merely a different legal path.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: No rule code forbids it. PUC10 says every capture must be "submitted **or** cancelled", which literally licenses submitting a to-be-cancelled capture; the Legal Outcomes table pairs "cancelled before submit" with CANCELLED but is described as a table of outcomes, not obligations. One implementer submits everything then cancels (getting "too-late" and reporting the submit-path state); another cancels first and reports CANCELLED. Different graded state for every `cancelTiming: before-submit` scenario.
readings: Submitting a before-submit-cancelled capture is a violation / wrong outcome; it must end CANCELLED.
It is not forbidden; the capture ends per its `outcome` knob and PUC10 is satisfied because it was submitted.

ambiguities.what: Whether a capture cancelled before submit can have a settlement record, and if it can, whether PUC4 or PUC7 wins.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: This is a direct counterexample to "The rules do not overlap ... **No precedence is needed and none is defined.**" The knob table lists `cancelTiming` and `settles` as independent knobs and carves out only `declined` captures as "always `never`" — nothing says a cancelled capture never settles. If the generator ever samples `cancelTiming: before-submit` with `settles: landed`, PUC4 demands the subject report CAPTURED while PUC7 and the transition table forbid any edge out of CANCELLED. The SPEC itself instructs me to flag this rather than resolve it.
readings: A never-submitted capture never gets a record (by analogy with the explicit `declined` carve-out), so the case never arises.
The knobs are genuinely independent, the case arises, and the rules send one capture to two different states with no defined precedence.

ambiguities.what: `PUC3_ONE_SUBMIT` says "**Exactly one** `submit` call per capture" while the facade section says "**At most one** `submit` call per capture per run".
ambiguities.whyItMatters: Under the literal PUC3 reading, a capture cancelled before submit (zero submit calls) violates PUC3 — meaning the CANCELLED legal outcome is unreachable without breaking a rule. Changes Q8 and the verdict on every cancellation scenario.
readings: "Exactly one" is loose prose for "at most one"; zero is fine on the cancel path.
"Exactly one" is normative, and the cancel path is a PUC3 violation — i.e. the SPEC contradicts itself.

ambiguities.what: What global ordering the flat `audit` array must have across multiple captures.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: `audit` is one array for all captures but the ordering constraint is written per capture ("One entry per transition **the capture** actually made, in the order they occurred"). With 2-4 captures, one implementer emits capture-grouped output (all of A's entries, then all of B's), another emits globally chronological interleaved output. If the grader diffs the array positionally, only one passes.
readings: Only each capture's own entries need to be in relative order; interleaving across captures is free.
The whole array must be in global chronological order of occurrence.

ambiguities.what: When a ledger-driven transition is deemed to "occur" — at the tick the record was written, or at the moment the subject reads `settlements()`.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: Compounds the previous item, and also decides whether an UNKNOWN->CAPTURED entry discovered after `tick()` returned `advanced: false` is a legal audit entry at all (the clock has stopped; PUC7-style reasoning could be read to say nothing further happens). Q9's required audit entry depends on this.
readings: Occurrence time = the subject's discovery, so the entry sorts after all tick-time events.
Occurrence time = the record's write tick, so entries must be back-dated and interleaved by `settlements()` write order.
Post-stop discoveries produce no audit entry at all, only a `decisions` state.

ambiguities.what: Whether records with `settleTick == clockBudget` are visible immediately after the last advancing `tick()`, or only after the call that returns `advanced: false`.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: An implementer who stops ticking when `remaining === 0` (never making the confirming non-advancing call) may miss last-tick records under the second reading and mis-report CAPTURED captures as UNKNOWN. "before `advanced` goes false" suggests the first reading but "which tick the record appears on" does not pin the read point.
readings: Visible as soon as the clockBudget-th tick returns; the extra tick is optional.
Visible only once the clock has actually stopped, so the extra non-advancing tick (or reading after `run`'s last statement) is required.

ambiguities.what: Whether the `idempotencyKey` and `amountMinor` passed to `submit` must be exactly the ones from `view.captures`, and what happens if they are not.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: PUC3 says "under its own key" but no rule says a wrong key is a violation, no rule says how the processor behaves with a foreign key, and `amountMinor` is never mentioned in the rules at all. An implementer could pass anything for `amountMinor` and the SPEC never says the run fails.
readings: Passing anything other than the capture's declared key/amount is a PUC3 (or unlisted) violation.
Only the call count is graded; arguments are ungraded and the processor keys off `captureId`.

ambiguities.what: Whether the grader inspects the facade call log or only the returned `decisions`/`audit`.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: Decides whether a subject may report CANCELLED (with a PENDING->CANCELLED audit entry) for a `before-submit` capture without ever calling `processor.cancel`, and symmetrically whether it may report SUBMITTED without calling `submit`. PUC10 says captures "must be submitted or cancelled", which sounds like a call-log check, but every other rule is phrased over the reported output.
readings: Call-log is checked: fabricating a state without the corresponding facade call fails.
Only the reported output is checked, and the call log matters solely for the PUC3 double-submit check.

ambiguities.what: Whether `PENDING` may ever legitimately appear as a reported `state`, and what `decisions` should say for a capture that is legally still PENDING (e.g. a run with no cancellation and a subject that chose not to submit).
ambiguities.whyItMatters: `state` is declared to be "one of the six state names" but PENDING is simultaneously declared not a legal final state and reporting it a failure. An implementer building a validator has to decide whether PENDING in `decisions` is a schema error or a rule violation, and which code it attributes.
readings: PENDING is schema-valid but always a PUC10 failure.
PENDING is simply never emittable and any occurrence is a malformed-output failure rather than a rule violation.

ambiguities.what: Behaviour for malformed or out-of-space input: duplicate `decisions` entries, a `decisions` entry for a captureId not in `view.captures`, a `cancellations` entry naming an unknown captureId, or `run` throwing.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: "Omitting a capture is a failure" is stated; the converse cases are not. A verifier that indexes decisions by captureId silently accepts duplicates and extras; one that compares sets rejects them.
readings: Extra/duplicate entries are ignored (last or first wins).
Extra/duplicate entries are a malformed-output failure.

ambiguities.what: Whether `tick()` calls beyond exhaustion, or repeated `settlements()` calls, are permitted without penalty.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: `settlements()` after stop is explicitly permitted; over-ticking is only described ("every later call returns the same") and never blessed as non-violating. A cautious implementer stops at `remaining === 0` and may therefore miss the confirming stop (see the settleTick == clockBudget item).
readings: Extra ticks are harmless; the description implies permission.
Only `clockBudget` ticks are sanctioned and extra calls could be counted as misuse of the facade.

ambiguities.what: What the subject must report if a terminal state is later contradicted (Q7's premise), or more generally what happens outside the seven edges.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: The SPEC asserts the case is impossible rather than defining an outcome, so there is no graded answer if a hidden scenario or a facade bug produces it. Any implementer writing defensive code has to invent a policy (keep terminal vs. follow the ledger), and the two policies give different `decisions`.
readings: Keep the terminal state, emit no further audit entry (PUC7 wins).
Follow the ledger and re-transition (PUC4/PUC9 win), emitting an edge that is not in the table.

ambiguities.what: Whether cancellations must be acted on in `view.cancellations` order, and whether "before-submit" means before that capture's submit or before any submit in the run.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: "`cancellations` names the captures the operator wants cancelled and **when the instruction becomes effective**" implies a timing semantics that is never defined against the subject's own call sequence. If it means "before any submit", a subject that submits capture 1 and then cancels capture 2 has violated an ordering constraint that no rule states.
readings: Per-capture: cancel that capture before submitting that capture; ordering relative to other captures is free.
Run-global: all before-submit cancellations must be issued before the first `submit` call of the run.

answers.question: Q1
answers.answer: UNKNOWN. The submit call performs two transitions inside the one call: PENDING -> SUBMITTED, then SUBMITTED -> UNKNOWN. SUBMITTED is a transient intermediate that must still be recorded in the audit, but the state the capture is *in* once submit has returned is UNKNOWN.
answers.specBasis: "**A `submit` call always moves the capture `PENDING -> SUBMITTED` first, whatever it returns.** The returned outcome then causes a second transition out of `SUBMITTED`, or none: ... `"timeout"` — `SUBMITTED -> UNKNOWN`." and "So a timeout produces **two** audit entries, `PENDING -> SUBMITTED` and `SUBMITTED -> UNKNOWN`."

answers.question: Q2
answers.answer: UNKNOWN.
answers.specBasis: `PUC5_UNRESOLVED_STAYS_UNKNOWN`: "If the clock stops with no settlement record for a capture whose `submit` returned `"timeout"`, its final state is `UNKNOWN` and the subject must report `UNKNOWN`."

answers.question: Q3
answers.answer: SUBMITTED. Not CAPTURED and not FAILED — an accepted-with-no-record capture ends in the non-terminal but legal final state SUBMITTED.
answers.specBasis: `PUC6_ACCEPTED_STAYS_SUBMITTED`: "If the clock stops with no settlement record for a capture whose `submit` returned `"accepted"`, its final state is `SUBMITTED` and the subject must report `SUBMITTED`. It becomes `CAPTURED` only on a `landed` record."

answers.question: Q4
answers.answer: Nothing that changes state. The subject may either skip `cancel` entirely or call `cancel(captureId)` and accept `"too-late"` — both are graded identically. The capture does NOT become CANCELLED (there is no UNKNOWN -> CANCELLED edge), no audit entry is produced (no transition occurred), and the reported state remains UNKNOWN unless a settlement record for its key resolves it to CAPTURED or FAILED. Note the SPEC also declares this case out of the sampled space.
answers.specBasis: "Calling `cancel` on a capture the subject has already submitted is not a violation — the correct response to a `while-unknown` cancellation is either to not call `cancel` at all, or to call it and accept `"too-late"`. Either is graded the same." plus "There is no `UNKNOWN -> CANCELLED` edge and no `SUBMITTED -> CANCELLED` edge."

answers.question: Q5
answers.answer: No. A second `submit` for that capture is a violation regardless of the key used, and the run is graded as failing. (The capture is also FAILED, which is terminal.)
answers.specBasis: "**At most one `submit` call per capture per run.** A second call for the same capture is a violation whatever key it uses, and the run is graded as failing."

answers.question: Q6
answers.answer: No. Same prohibition — the violation is per capture, not per key.
answers.specBasis: "A second call for the same capture is a violation whatever key it uses, and the run is graded as failing." and `PUC3_ONE_SUBMIT`: "Exactly one `submit` call per capture, under its own key. A second call is a violation."

answers.question: Q7
answers.answer: The SPEC declares this case impossible, so it prescribes no behavior for it. If it nevertheless occurred, the two governing rules point in opposite directions and the SPEC explicitly refuses to arbitrate: PUC7 says CAPTURED is terminal with no outgoing edge (so: keep reporting CAPTURED), while PUC9 says the report must be consistent with the ledger (so: FAILED). The SPEC's own instruction for this situation is to treat it as a SPEC defect, not a judgement call. Best-supported answer: CAPTURED, because no edge leaves a terminal state and the table has no CAPTURED -> FAILED transition.
answers.specBasis: "**The ledger holds at most one record per key, and a record never changes once written.** There is no case in which two records for one key disagree." and "If you find a capture that two rules send to different states, that is a defect in this SPEC and not a judgement call for you to make."

answers.question: Q8
answers.answer: Zero or one. Exactly one for every capture the subject submits, using that capture's own idempotency key; zero for a capture the subject cancels before submitting (PENDING -> CANCELLED). A second call for the same capture is always a violation. Note the SPEC states this two incompatible ways: 'At most one' (permits zero) versus PUC3's 'Exactly one submit call per capture' (permits no zero-submit path), reconciled only by PUC10's disjunction 'submitted or cancelled'.
answers.specBasis: "**At most one `submit` call per capture per run.**" vs `PUC3_ONE_SUBMIT`: "Exactly one `submit` call per capture, under its own key." vs `PUC10_DRIVE_EVERY_CAPTURE`: "Every capture in `view.captures` must be submitted or cancelled"

answers.question: Q9
answers.answer: Must resolve it — it is not too late. Reading `settlements()` after the clock has stopped is explicitly permitted, and the record's presence at clock-stop obliges the subject to report the state it names (CAPTURED for `landed`, FAILED for `not-landed`), plus the corresponding UNKNOWN -> CAPTURED / UNKNOWN -> FAILED audit entry. Reporting UNKNOWN in this case is listed as an illegal outcome.
answers.specBasis: `PUC4_RESOLVE_WHEN_ANSWERED`: "If a settlement record for a capture's key is in `settlements()` at the moment the clock stops, the subject must report the state that record names." and "Calling it after the clock has stopped is permitted and returns the final ledger." and Illegal Outcomes: "Reporting `UNKNOWN` for a capture whose record was in `settlements()` when the clock stopped."

answers.question: Q10
answers.answer: Exactly seven: PENDING->SUBMITTED (subject calls submit); PENDING->CANCELLED (subject calls cancel on an unsubmitted capture); SUBMITTED->CAPTURED (landed record); SUBMITTED->FAILED ('declined' return, or a not-landed record); SUBMITTED->UNKNOWN ('timeout' return); UNKNOWN->CAPTURED (landed record); UNKNOWN->FAILED (not-landed record). SUBMITTED -> CANCELLED is NOT legal. Also absent by design: PENDING->UNKNOWN, UNKNOWN->CANCELLED, and any edge out of CAPTURED/FAILED/CANCELLED.
answers.specBasis: "The legal transitions are exactly these seven and no others" and "There is no `UNKNOWN -> CANCELLED` edge and no `SUBMITTED -> CANCELLED` edge. A capture that has been submitted cannot be cancelled, whatever its outcome."

answers.question: Q11
answers.answer: CANCELLED, via the single audit entry PENDING -> CANCELLED. No settlement record is required or expected — PUC9 demands ledger support only for CAPTURED and FAILED, and the capture was never submitted.
answers.specBasis: "`cancel(captureId)` returns `"cancelled"` and moves the capture `PENDING -> CANCELLED` if the capture has not been submitted." and Legal Outcomes: "cancelled before submit | `CANCELLED`" and `PUC9`: "`CAPTURED` requires a `landed` record, `FAILED` requires either a `not-landed` record or a `"declined"` outcome"

answers.question: Q12
answers.answer: It cannot happen — the SPEC declares keys and captures one-to-one and guarantees a record names exactly one capture. The SPEC prescribes NOTHING for the violated case: there is no rule telling the subject to detect the collision, no defined attribution when one record names two captures, and no defined report. NOTHING IN THE SPEC.
answers.specBasis: "**Idempotency keys and captures are one-to-one.** Each capture has exactly one key for its whole life, and no key is ever shared by two captures. A settlement record naming a key therefore names exactly one capture." — nothing states behavior when this invariant is violated.

answers.question: Q13
answers.answer: An empty array.
answers.specBasis: "Before any `tick()` it returns an empty array."

answers.question: Q14
answers.answer: The SPEC never obliges the subject to call `tick()` — 'The clock budget is the subject's to spend' — but not ticking makes PUC4 unsatisfiable in every scenario whose knobs write a record, so in practice the subject must tick until the clock stops. How many: spend the whole budget, i.e. call `tick()` until it returns `advanced: false` (equivalently, `view.clockBudget` advancing ticks, since `settleTick` ranges 1..clockBudget). What the SPEC does NOT settle is whether a subject that ticks zero or too few times and then correctly reports UNKNOWN/SUBMITTED passes (literal PUC5/PUC6 compliance) or fails (violating the 'must not refuse to decide' mandate) — that is a guess.
answers.specBasis: "A subject that never calls `tick()` has stopped the clock at zero and will see an empty ledger. The clock budget is the subject's to spend." and "A run whose knobs say a capture settles will have its record visible in `settlements()` before `advanced` goes false, provided the subject spends its ticks." — no rule states the subject MUST spend them.

answers.question: Q15
answers.answer: SUBMITTED. Same as Q3 (yes — identical rule, PUC6). NOT the same as Q2, which is UNKNOWN: the discriminator is what `submit` returned ('accepted' -> SUBMITTED, 'timeout' -> UNKNOWN), not the absence of the record, which is common to both.
answers.specBasis: `PUC6_ACCEPTED_STAYS_SUBMITTED`: "If the clock stops with no settlement record for a capture whose `submit` returned `"accepted"`, its final state is `SUBMITTED`..." vs `PUC5_UNRESOLVED_STAYS_UNKNOWN`: "...for a capture whose `submit` returned `"timeout"`, its final state is `UNKNOWN`..."

ambiguities.what: The shape of a settlement record object is never specified. `settlements()` is the pivot of the entire task, but the SPEC says only that a record 'names an idempotency key and says landed or not-landed' — it never gives the field names or value spelling. Every other data structure in the SPEC (view, decisions, audit, tick's return) is given as literal JS; this one is prose only.

Record is {key, landed: boolean}
Record is keyed by captureId rather than idempotencyKey (the SPEC says keys and captures are 1:1, so an implementer could assume either identifier is present)

PUC4 is evaluated against the run's knob-determined ground truth — under-ticking is a PUC4 failure disguised as PUC5/PUC6 compliance

The SPEC's only statement, 'Every settlement record that will ever be written is written by the time the clock stops', is silent on causation.
readings: Records are written on their settleTick unconditionally, so tick-then-submit still sees them
Records are only written for captures already submitted, so tick-then-submit sees an empty ledger and every capture reports SUBMITTED/UNKNOWN
Submit-then-tick is the only intended order and other orders are out of the space

ambiguities.whyItMatters: This is a direct collision inside the region the SPEC swears is collision-free. The SPEC says 'No precedence is needed and none is defined', so there is no tiebreak.
readings: Report CANCELLED — terminal wins, and the record is for a key the subject never submitted
Report CAPTURED/FAILED — PUC4 is unconditional about records present at clock stop
The combination is implicitly excluded by construction and will never be sampled

ambiguities.what: Whether the `audit` array must be globally chronologically ordered across captures, or only per-capture ordered. The SPEC says 'in the order they occurred' about the transitions of a capture, but the array is a single flat global list.

A verifier doing exact array comparison passes one and fails the other; PUC8 is silent.
readings: Global chronological order required
Per-capture order required, grouping by capture allowed
Any order in which each capture's own entries are relatively ordered

ambiguities.what: When a ledger-driven transition is deemed to 'occur' for audit purposes: at the tick on which the record was written, or at the moment the subject reads `settlements()`.

readings: Transition occurs when the record is written (subject must poll each tick to order correctly)
Transition occurs when the subject observes the record
Only relative per-capture order matters, so it is moot

ambiguities.what: `while-unknown` is declared as a live value of `view.cancellations[].when` in the interface AND gets a dedicated paragraph of correct-response guidance in the `cancel` section, but the Declared Knobs table says '`while-unknown` is not in the space'.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: An implementer who trusts the knob table may not handle the value at all (crash, or silently skip); one who trusts the interface handles it. If any hidden scenario emits it — including as a trap for exactly this contradiction — the two implementations diverge completely.

while-unknown can appear; the knob table only means it is not a *graded* variable
while-unknown appears specifically as a no-op robustness probe

ambiguities.what: No rule requires the subject to HONOR a `before-submit` cancellation. PUC10 states the obligation as a disjunction ('must be submitted or cancelled'), and nothing says submitting a capture named in `cancellations` is a violation, nor that cancelling a capture NOT named in `cancellations` is one.
ambiguities.whyItMatters: A subject that ignores `view.cancellations` entirely and submits everything satisfies PUC10, PUC3 and PUC8 by the letter — the cancelled capture just ends SUBMITTED/CAPTURED/UNKNOWN instead of CANCELLED. Symmetrically, a subject that cancels every capture also satisfies PUC10. Whether either is a failure is nowhere stated; only the Legal Outcomes table's row 'cancelled before submit | CANCELLED' hints at an obligation, and that table describes outcomes, not duties.
readings: Cancellation instructions are binding: a before-submit capture MUST end CANCELLED
Cancellation instructions are advisory: any outcome consistent with the transition table passes
Submitting a before-submit-cancelled capture is a violation but cancelling an uninstructed capture is not (or vice versa)

ambiguities.what: 'At most one `submit` call per capture per run' contradicts PUC3's 'Exactly one `submit` call per capture'.

An implementer resolving the conflict toward PUC3 would submit every capture including the cancelled ones (then cancel, getting 'too-late'), producing entirely different final states for cancelled captures.
readings: 'At most one' governs; zero submits is correct for cancelled captures
